projects.title: Cloud EEG Ingestion & Analysis Platform
projects.headline: Reading the part of an EEG recording a viewer needs.
projects.summary: A five-service backend for storing, processing and streaming EEG recordings.

facets.Problem: EEG recordings can be too large to load into memory at once. The platform needed to ingest them, run analysis, export results and let a viewer request a short section of the signal.
facets.Built: I worked on a five-service platform with 50+ APIs. PostgreSQL and TimescaleDB hold structured data; Azure Blob Storage holds large files. Redis coordinates background jobs. The streaming path reads the requested time window rather than loading the whole recording. I also set up and ran the production and test environments on Azure: Docker Swarm services, CI/CD releases, versioned schema migrations and Prometheus/Grafana monitoring.
facets.Tradeoff: Heavy analysis runs outside the HTTP request. Object storage replaces local disk. Live viewing has to share resources with batch frequency-band analysis and EDF+/PDF export jobs, so those workloads are scheduled separately. A worker leases each job and sends heartbeats while it runs; if the heartbeats stop, an atomic requeue puts the job back, so a restart neither loses nor duplicates work.
facets.Evidence: Bounded time-window streaming cancels stale requests when the viewer moves on. A binary format that groups values by column cut the payload per chunk from about 1.3 MB to 288 KB. Profiling took median (p50) first-chunk latency from roughly 2.2 s to 783 ms, and server send time from about 250 ms to 12 ms. Database fetches account for 87% of the remaining time. The sleep-analysis service processes a recording in memory-bounded chunks: a 24-hour recording went from 157.6 s to 32.6 s with identical results, and a 50-hour, 32-channel study completed. I led the investigation into a drift reported against a reference clinical viewer. Our traces matched the raw EDF recording at a correlation above 0.999; the drift was an 18.3% difference in display scale, not a sample delay.

projects.title: MediPredict ML Microservice
projects.headline: The model scored well with an input it could not have.
projects.summary: An insurance prediction service and an audit of a misleading result.

facets.Problem: Predict an insurance premium from information available when a new applicant asks for a quote. A strong offline score is little use if the model needs information that arrives later.
facets.Built: I built the FastAPI ML microservice: typed prediction schemas, model loading from saved artifacts, preprocessing shared with training, health and readiness endpoints, SHAP feature explanations and Docker packaging. The rest of the team built the Spring Boot backend and React frontend that call it. Those parts are not my work.
facets.Tradeoff: I separated inputs available at quote time from signals available at renewal. Realised annual medical cost belongs to the latter. Histogram gradient boosting replaced random forest in the served model; SHAP exposes how features affect its predictions.
facets.Evidence: The reported R² of 0.925 used realised annual medical cost, which does not exist when a new applicant receives a quote. R² measures fit against a mean-only prediction; it is not a percentage accuracy. Removing unavailable features while holding the model fixed put the quote-time result near R² 0.15. A cross-dataset audit reproduced the collapse while leaving leakage-free datasets untouched. Replacing random forest with histogram gradient boosting cut the served artifact from 95.8 MB to 0.39 MB and single-row inference from roughly 45 ms to 0.5 ms, at unchanged cross-validated accuracy. I first-authored the paper on this finding. It has been accepted at ICIDA 2026 (Springer LNNS); presentation and publication are pending.

projects.title: EEG Signal-Processing Benchmark
projects.headline: A fast EEG window can still give the wrong answer.
projects.summary: Checking whether a filtered window matches the whole recording, then timing it.

facets.Problem: Processing an EEG recording in small windows can silently change the result. I wanted to find where window boundaries, padding and scheduling break equivalence with processing the whole recording.
facets.Built: A reproducible benchmark for random-access EEG filtering, written with NumPy, SciPy and MNE and run on 53 validated recordings from five public datasets (CHB-MIT, Sleep-EDF, HMC, CAP and BDSP). It reports three things separately: whether a library call is valid for the input, which fallback the application chooses when it is not, and how much error that choice introduces.
facets.Tradeoff: Reading two seconds of real signal on each side of a window costs extra work on every request, so the benchmark measures that cost instead of assuming it. It times each window directly. It does not establish how much traffic a complete service can handle.
facets.Evidence: With two seconds of real context per side, the error where one window meets the next fell from 3.80–23.53 µV to below 0.001 µV, and band-power distortion fell from up to 6.17 to below 0.001 percentage points. On the slowest recording, the 95th-percentile (p95) signal-processing time per window was 2.37 ms. The benchmark also records where windowed processing breaks: inputs too short for a filter, timing error when the application falls back to a one-directional (causal) filter, artifacts at window joins and spectral leakage near band edges. A revision has been submitted to the IEEE SPMB 2026 abstract and poster track.

projects.title: Local-First RAG Chatbot
projects.headline: Search that shows how it ranked the results.
projects.summary: Local document search that combines meaning with exact-term matches.

facets.Problem: Search private documents without sending them to a hosted service. The interface, command line and programmatic clients need to expose how retrieval chose its results.
facets.Built: FAISS finds documents with similar meaning through vector search. BM25 ranks exact-term matches. Reciprocal Rank Fusion combines their positions in the two lists. SQLite stores metadata, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server gives clients structured access.
facets.Tradeoff: The local store has one writer. That keeps updates and retrieval behaviour easier to inspect, at the cost of distributed scale.
facets.Evidence: On a fixed synthetic set of 18 queries, hybrid search kept Hit Rate@3 at 1.000 and raised mean reciprocal rank (MRR) from 0.972 to 1.000. Hit Rate@3 asks whether the expected result appears in the first three; MRR rewards finding it nearer the top. This is a regression guard, not a general quality benchmark.

projects.title: Tempo Priority Assistant
projects.headline: A model drafts the task. Code sets the schedule.
projects.summary: A local planning assistant with date handling outside the language model.

facets.Problem: Turn loosely written tasks into a feasible daily plan without giving a language model control over dates, files or external actions.
facets.Built: React and Express pass schema-constrained output from a local Ollama model to a typed Python service. That service resolves relative dates and schedules tasks.
facets.Tradeoff: Inference runs serially to fit limited video memory (VRAM). Explicit tool permissions restrict what the model can request. This limits flexibility but makes the behaviour easier to inspect.
facets.Evidence: Locked Node and Python test suites run in CI. They cover scheduling, queue cancellation, provider failures, tool policy and persistence in the browser.

projects.title: Nand2Tetris Hardware Stack & Two-Pass Assembler
projects.headline: From NAND gates to 16-bit machine code.
projects.summary: The Nand2Tetris hardware stack and a two-pass assembler written in Python.

facets.Problem: Build the hardware of a small computer from basic logic gates, then translate Hack assembly into 16-bit machine code.
facets.Built: Logic gates written in a hardware description language (HDL), an arithmetic logic unit (ALU), memory, a program counter and memory-mapped input/output. The Python assembler separates parsing, code generation, symbol handling and orchestration.
facets.Tradeoff: Explicit translation tables keep instruction encoding readable. A first pass records label addresses; a second resolves symbols and emits instructions. I used Python so I could write and inspect the translation rather than copy the tutorial implementation.
facets.Evidence: Built through the hardware portion, reached 16K memory, implemented an ALU capable of 18 operations via 6 control bits, and generated .hack binaries from .asm programs.

projects.title: Premiere Assist CLI
projects.summary: Local media analysis becomes an edit plan you can review. FFmpeg supplies the evidence; a deterministic resolver validates candidate IDs and writes an edit decision list and Premiere delivery package. The model never executes a command. Batch export runs natively in Premiere Pro through an Adobe CEP extension, with durable job claims and a full decode of every output; one recording has produced six portrait reels. Editorial quality still needs evaluation.

projects.title: NewsTrellis Evidence Organizer
projects.summary: Organises RSS and Atom feeds into a finite daily reading list while keeping sources and corrections attached. Ingestion requires approval, validates URLs against server-side request forgery (SSRF), removes duplicates and groups related items, and articles open in a sanitized in-app reader. The suite has 166 automated tests and 25 browser layout checks; the interface still needs broader usability testing.

projects.title: Internal RAG Knowledge Assistant
projects.summary: Built during my Aecho AI internship. A Python pipeline ingests 300+ pages of internal documentation. A Streamlit interface retrieves relevant passages before answering with a local model in LM Studio. Sensitive material stays local; routine lookup fell from minutes to seconds.

bio_html:
I build backend systems for data that does not fit in memory, and for models that should not be trusted blindly.

I did not set out to work on brains. I set out to work as a backend engineer, and the role that found me happened to involve EEG. Clinical recordings can be large enough for one careless query to exhaust memory. Processing them in windows can change the result without throwing an error. Someone may use that output to make a decision about a patient.

Models propose. Deterministic code decides.

In Tempo, a local model drafts tasks but a typed Python service owns the dates and schedule. In Premiere Assist, FFmpeg supplies evidence to a resolver that writes the edit list; the model never runs a command. My retrieval system exposes how semantic and exact-term search contribute to each result. I trade flexibility for behaviour I can reproduce and explain.

I would rather write down a decision than assume everyone has the same context. The expensive failures I have watched were rarely technical; they were two people each confident they had already agreed.

My final-year insurance project became a leakage audit when the offline score looked too good. The EEG benchmark came from checking whether processing a short window gave the same answer as processing the whole recording. Those questions are why I keep the measurement conditions beside the numbers.

The habit I am working against is overengineering: building for a scale and a set of cases a system may never meet. Naming it has not cured it, but it has made me slower to reach for the abstraction.
